ta-l1d23q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 23. Having divided the divine names, Lombard excepts 'person' from the general rule, since it is said according to substance yet predicated in the plural. He shows that 'person' signifies substance (Augustine) and then asks the reason for the exception: why 'person' is predicated plurally of several persons, given the necessity, for Latins with 'person' and Greeks with 'hypostasis', of some substance-name predicated plurally to answer the question 'three what?'; and why other essential names, like 'God' or 'essence', are not predicated plurally. He proves that in God there is neither diversity, which is why 'essence' is not plural, nor singularity, which is why 'person' is. Four articles are announced: the distinction of essence, subsistence, substance, and person and their Greek counterparts usia, usiosis, hypostasis, prosopon; whether 'person' is properly said of God; whether it signifies substance or relation; and, if it signifies substance in some way, whether it is predicated plurally.
claims: 'Person' is said according to substance yet predicated in the plural.
In God there is neither diversity (so no plural 'essences') nor singularity (so plural 'persons').

ta-l1d23q1-d1e131.summary: First argument that the four names are synonyms. Boethius says usia signifies composite substance, which is the individual subsisting in the genus of substance, signified by 'substance', 'hypostasis', or 'person', so 'essence' or 'usia' does not differ in meaning from the others.
claims: Usia signifies composite substance.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e134.summary: Second argument. Only what has complete being in itself subsists, and complete being is found only in the particular, since universals have being apart from particulars only in the soul, which is incomplete being. The particular in the genus of substance is called hypostasis or first substance, so subsistence is the same as substance.
claims: Only particulars subsist.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e137.summary: Third argument. Both 'subsist' and 'substand' imply something placed under something, so they are the same.
claims: Subsistere and substare both imply being under.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e141.summary: Fourth argument. Boethius says the Greeks use 'hypostasis' only for an individual of rational nature, which is called a person, so hypostasis and prosopon, or substance and person, are the same.
claims: Greeks use hypostasis only for rational individuals.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e144.summary: Fifth argument. As the Greeks say three hypostases, we say three substances, not three subsistences as they say three usioses, so our 'subsistence' is the same as their 'hypostasis', contrary to Boethius in De duabus naturis.
claims: Latin and Greek terms seem mismatched.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e147.summary: Sed contra from Boethius, who distinguishes the meanings of these names, and from Cicero, whom Boethius cites.
claims: Boethius distinguishes the four names.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e150.summary: Thomas's determination. The four names differ in meaning, though their difference is assigned variously. Some take it from what is common and distinct in God. The common is signified as quo est (essence) or quod est (subsistence), or as giving being to all (essence) or having self-sufficient being (subsistence), while the distinct is signified concretely (person) or abstractly (hypostasis), or as distinguishable (hypostasis) or distinguished (person), or as distinguished by a property of dignity (person) or by any property (hypostasis). Thomas rejects this: even without distinction in God these names would apply without being synonyms, and parts are false. God is not called essence because he gives being, any more than wise because he gives wisdom, but rather gives being because he has essence, as fire heats because it has heat; God, as pure act, has nothing signifiable as potency not joined to act, so nothing distinguishable versus distinguished; and hypostasis does not signify the proper in abstraction, which is what a property-name like 'paternity' signifies. Others take the difference from quo est and quod est, some making three signify quo est (essence the generic nature, subsistence the specific, hypostasis the individual) and person signify quod est, others the reverse, with essence as quo est and the other three as quod est in different respects, and others with two of each. But since each name except 'person' is sometimes used for quo est and sometimes for quod est, none of these is an essential distinction. So, following Boethius, the difference of 'essence', 'subsistence', and 'substance' should be taken from the acts they are imposed from: to be (esse), to subsist (subsistere), and to stand under (substare). To be is common and determines no mode of being; to subsist is a determinate mode of being, being through itself and not in another, like an accident; to stand under is to be placed under another. Being is common to all genera, while subsisting and standing under are proper to the first category, as being complete in itself and as underlying all accidents. So essence is that whose act is to be, subsistence that whose act is to subsist, and substance that whose act is to stand under. Each act can belong to something as quod est, as heating belongs to what heats, or as quo est, as heating belongs to heat. When something follows several things that come together, it is denominated not from one of them, even its principle, but from the whole, as flavour follows the hot and the moist together and something is called flavoured not from heat but from flavour. Since being follows the composition of matter and form, though form is its principle, a thing is called a being not from the form but from the whole, so essence in material composites signifies the whole, also called quiddity and nature, which is why Boethius says usia signifies a composite of matter and form. But this nature, though composed of matter and form, is not composed of this designated matter under determinate accidents, in which the form is individuated, which 'Socrates' signifies; designated matter is like the recipient of the common nature. So nature or essence is signified as a part, when the common nature is taken precisively, excluding whatever does not belong to it, as 'humanity', which is not predicated and is neither genus nor species but that by which man is formally named; or as a whole, when what belongs to the common nature is understood non-precisively, so that designated matter is included potentially, as 'man', signified as quod est. 'Essence' is used both ways: sometimes we say Socrates is an essence, sometimes that Socrates' essence is not Socrates. Likewise subsisting belongs to something as what subsists or as that by which it subsists. Since subsisting is determinate being, and all determination of being follows form, something is called subsisting by its first form in the genus of substance, as white by whiteness, so Boethius calls usiosis or subsistence the form receiving subsistence, that by which something subsists. Taken for what subsists, subsistence belongs first to what such a nature with this mode of being is found in first: genera and species in the genus of substance, and individuals only as under such a common nature, since although genera and species subsist only in individuals, whose being it is, the determination of being comes from the higher nature or quiddity. Likewise hypostasis or substance is said in two ways: that by which something stands under, whose first principle is matter, so Boethius says hypostasis is matter; or what stands under, which is first the individual in the genus of substance, since genera and species stand under accidents only through individuals, so 'substance' belongs first and principally to particular substances (the Philosopher, Boethius). So taken as quo est, essence signifies the quiddity as form of the whole, usiosis the form of the part, and hypostasis matter. Taken as quod est, one and the same thing is called essence as having being, subsistence as having such being, absolute being, which belongs first to genera and species, and substance as standing under accidents, which belongs first to individuals. 'Person' signifies a particular substance as subject to a property signifying dignity, like prosopon among the Greeks, so there is person only in intellectual nature. According to Boethius 'persona' comes from 'personare', from the masks worn in tragedies and comedies to represent those whose deeds were sung, and by usage every human individual of whom such a story can be told came to be called a person; prosopon likewise comes from 'pro' (before) and 'sopos' (face), since such masks were put before the face.
claims: Essence, subsistence, and substance are distinguished by the acts they are named from: to be, to subsist, to stand under.
Each can be taken as quo est (form of the whole, form of the part, matter) or as quod est (thing having being, having absolute being, underlying accidents).
Essence taken precisively (humanity) is a part; taken non-precisively (man) is the whole.
'Person' is a particular substance of intellectual nature under a property of dignity; the name comes from theatrical masks.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e153.summary: Reply to the first argument. The particular signifies a composite of matter and designated form, while the universal in composite substances also signifies a composite of matter and form, but not designated, as man is from soul, flesh, and bone, but not from this flesh and these bones. So usia need not mean the same as particular substance; it relates to both, and whatever is in the genus of substance, universal or particular, can be called usia.
claims: Usia applies to both universal and particular substances.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e156.summary: Reply to the second argument. 'To subsist' implies being and a determinate mode of being. Being simply belongs only to individuals, but the determination of being comes from the nature or quiddity of genus or species. So although genera and species exist only in individuals, subsisting properly belongs to them and they are called subsistences, though the particular is too, but secondarily, as species are called substances, but second substances.
claims: Genera and species are subsistences primarily, as determining the mode of being.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e160.summary: Reply to the third argument. Something is called substance as standing under an accident or a common nature, but it is said to subsist as being under its own being, not as having being in another as in a subject.
claims: Substare is to underlie accidents; subsistere is to be under one's own being.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e163.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Among the Greeks 'hypostasis' has one thing from its proper signification and another from usage. By signification it means any particular substance, but by usage it is reserved to nobler substances, so they use 'hypostasis' as we use 'person', which is not our usage of 'substance'.
claims: Hypostasis means any particular substance by signification but is used like 'person'.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e166.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Among us 'substance' is equivocal: sometimes it stands for essence, as when we say a definition signifies a thing's substance, and sometimes for the supposit of a substance, as when we say Socrates is a substance. To prevent misunderstanding, the saints would not use 'substance' for the supposit as the Greeks do but transposed the terms, making 'subsistence' correspond to hypostasis and 'substance' to usiosis, though in truth of signification it is the reverse; they cared more about avoiding errors than about the propriety of names.
claims: The Latin Fathers transposed 'substance' and 'subsistence' to avoid misunderstanding, against strict signification.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e178.summary: First argument that 'person' is not properly said of God. 'Person' signifies a masked man whose figure is represented, which can fit God only metaphorically, and God has no figure to represent ('to whom have you likened God?', Isa. 40:18).
claims: Persona originally signifies a masked actor.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e184.summary: Second argument. In all of nature, a person seems to involve the greatest composition, since nearly all natures come together in a human individual, in soul and body, which is why the human is said to share something with everything. God is supremely simple.
claims: The human person is the most composite being.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e187.summary: Third argument. A person is what stands under a property or subsists, and God is not properly said to stand under anything in him (Augustine, Dist. 8).
claims: God stands under nothing.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e191.summary: Fourth argument. 'Person' signifies a particular or singular substance, and particular or singular does not fit God.
claims: Particularity does not fit God.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e194.summary: Sed contra. 'Persona' is said as 'per se una', one through itself, which fits God most of all.
claims: Persona as per se una.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e197.summary: Second sed contra. 'Person' signifies something complete existing in intellectual nature, which fits God.
claims: Person is something complete in intellectual nature.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e200.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Person' properly fits God, though not in the same way as in creatures but more nobly, as with everything said of God and creatures. The concept of person is preserved in God as having being subsisting through itself in intellectual nature.
claims: 'Person' is said properly of God, as subsisting through itself in intellectual nature, more nobly than in creatures.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e203.summary: Reply to the first argument. In a name's signification two things must be considered: that from which the name is imposed and that which it is imposed to signify. A thing's substance is sometimes named from an accident that does not follow its whole nature, as 'lapis' (stone) is said from 'laedere pedem' (hurting the foot), though not everything that hurts the foot is a stone or conversely. So a name is judged not by what it is imposed from but by what it is instituted to signify. Although 'person' was imposed from theatrical representation, it was imposed to signify a complete substance subsisting in intellectual nature, which fits God, though what it was imposed from does not.
claims: Names are judged by what they are imposed to signify, not by what they are imposed from.
concepts: id a quo vs. id ad quod nomen imponitur

ta-l1d23q1-d1e206.summary: Reply to the second argument. That composition is incidental to the concept of person. Since 'person' means something complete in intellectual nature, and in human nature completeness is found only through the greatest composition, it signifies composition only incidentally. If intellectual perfection were found in a simple body like fire, it would be called a person, so divine simplicity does not conflict with personhood.
claims: Composition is incidental to the concept of person.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e210.summary: Reply to the third argument. In God nothing is placed under anything in reality, only in our mode of understanding, as he is understood to stand under a property, personal or essential, and so is called substance, and to be under (being), and so is called subsistence. Still, because in reality nothing there is under another, Richard of St Victor, wishing to speak properly, says that the divine persons do not subsist but exist, inasmuch as they are distinguished by properties of origin, by which one is from another, and do not underlie them as a subject. So he calls the divine persons not subsistences but existences.
claims: God stands under properties only in our mode of understanding.
Richard of St Victor calls the persons 'existences' rather than 'subsistences'.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e213.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Strictly, there is no particular in God, since something is called particular because a common nature is particularized in it, receiving part of the nature according to the power by which it can be in many, though it receives its whole concept. In the Father the divine nature is according to its whole power, so he cannot be called particular, except perhaps by reason of numerical multitude (Dist. 19, Damascene). Likewise 'God' cannot be particular or singular, since it is predicated of several supposits and lacks matter, the principle of singularity. So 'person' is said of God not by the concept of particularity or singularity but by the concept of completeness, as naming something complete subsisting or existing in intellectual nature.
claims: 'Person' is said of God by the concept of completeness, not particularity.
In God the nature is in each person by its whole power, so no person is a 'particular'.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e225.summary: First argument that 'person' signifies substance, from Augustine in the text, who seems to say this expressly.
claims: Augustine says 'person' signifies substance.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e228.summary: Second argument from Boethius's definition: a person is an individual substance of rational nature. Substance signifies something absolute, not relative, so 'person' does not signify relation.
claims: Boethius defines person as rationalis naturae individua substantia.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e234.summary: Third argument. Every relative is referred to another by its name, and 'person' is not, so it does not signify relation.
claims: Relatives are referred to another by name.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e238.summary: Fourth argument. 'What' asks about substance or essence, and to the heretics asking 'three what?' the answer was 'persons' (Father, Son, and Spirit), so 'person' signifies essence.
claims: 'Quid' asks about essence.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e241.summary: Fifth argument. 'Person' is said as 'one through itself', and one signifies essence.
claims: Unity signifies essence.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e244.summary: Sed contra from Boethius: every name that takes its origin from the persons certainly does not pertain to substance, and no name takes its origin from the persons as much as 'person'.
claims: Names originating from the persons do not pertain to substance.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e250.summary: Second sed contra. The Father is distinguished from the Son in nothing absolute, only by relation, and he is distinguished in person, so 'person' signifies relation, not something absolute. The premise follows from divine simplicity and the perfection of the whole Trinity.
claims: The persons are distinguished only by relation.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e253.summary: Third sed contra. Whatever genus an inferior reduces to, its superior reduces to as well. Father, Son, and Spirit fall under 'person', and 'Father' signifies a relation, so 'person' does too.
claims: Inferior and superior belong to the same genus.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e256.summary: Thomas's determination. Doctors hold many views on the meaning of 'person'. Some say it is equivocal: by time (signifying the essence before the heretics' question, then essence in the singular and relation in the plural, and after Boethius relation in both), which is unreasonable, since the plural is the doubled singular with the same signification; by different significates (sometimes essence, sometimes hypostasis, sometimes property, as Lombard seems to hold in Dist. 26), none of which gives the full meaning, since 'person' includes all; or by adjuncts (substance alone, relation with a partitive or numeral term), which fails because absolute substance-names do not admit such additions ('several gods'). Others say it is univocal: signifying only substance, the hypostasis or first substance, which does not suffice, since nothing absolute is numbered in God; signifying two things, one directly and one obliquely (relation directly and substance obliquely, or the reverse); or signifying both principally, either with the property placed on the substance as distinguishing it, though it is not easy to see how something absolute is distinguished in God, or without that, though it is not clear how one name signifies several things unless they make one. To see what is true in each, note that 'person' signifies an individual substance. An individual can be signified by a second-intention name ('individual', 'singular'), which signifies the intention of singularity, not the singular thing, or by a first-intention name signifying the thing to which particularity belongs, as 'person' does. So one can speak of the meaning of 'person' in itself or as found in this or that nature. In itself it signifies an individual intellectual substance, whatever it is and however individuated. A human person is what subsists in human nature, distinguished as fits human nature, by determinate matter. Here we speak of the divine person, so it signifies what is distinct existing in the divine nature. By the necessity of faith, which confesses God three and one, there must be something common by which they are one, the essence or divine nature signified by 'deity', and something proper that distinguishes, from which they are three, a relation such as paternity. Since there is no composition in God, deity must be really the same as God, and paternity as Father. Of the four, deity, God, Father, paternity, deity as signified as a nature does not have the character of person, because it is not signified as subsistent and because it is common, while a person is something distinct. 'God' does not either: though signified as subsistent, it is not distinct, since Father and Son agree in being God as in deity. If the plurality of persons were removed, and with it the commonness of 'God', then 'God' would signify a person distinct from all other natures by essential properties. 'Paternity' is signified not as subsistent or as distinct but as distinguishing, so not as a person. 'Father', though signified as distinct, is signified not as subsisting in a nature but as subject of a property, so like 'white' it is not a name of person by its concept. But since Father and God are the same, not as accident and subject but by total indifference of reality, the Father, as Father who is God, is a person. So 'person' in God signifies relation by way of substance. The distinguishing relation is the distinct thing, since paternity is the Father, and since 'person' signifies something distinct existing in a nature, it signifies relation insofar as the relation is the related thing itself and the related thing subsists in such a nature. So 'person' signifies relation by way of substance, not the substance that is essence but the supposit having the essence. Each opinion says something true. Those who called it equivocal were right that 'person' includes property, hypostasis, and essence, which do not differ really in God, so it can stand for one or another, though this happens because they are one in reality. Those who said it signifies only hypostasis attended to its mode of signifying, as subsisting in a nature, though it signifies the distinct thing, the distinguishing relation. Those who said it signifies substance directly attended to substance as hypostasis distinguished by a property; those who said the reverse attended to substance as essence. Those who said it signifies hypostasis with a property placed on it took hypostasis not as subsisting in the divine nature, signified by 'God' and common to the three, but as the distinguishing relation itself, since in God distinguishing and distinguished are the same; those who denied the property is placed on the substance as distinguishing it considered hypostasis or substance in the other way.
claims: 'Person' in itself signifies an individual intellectual substance; the divine person signifies what is distinct existing in the divine nature.
'Person' in God signifies relation by way of substance: the subsistent relation, as supposit having the essence.
Deity, God, paternity, and Father taken by their concepts are not 'person'; the Father is a person as Father who is God.
The competing opinions are each partly true, given the real identity of essence, hypostasis, and property in God.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e260.summary: Reply to the first argument. Augustine attends to the meaning of 'person' as to its mode of signifying, not to what it signifies. Although it signifies relation, it signifies it by way of substance, so he said it signifies substance, and since substance in God is the same as essence, it follows that it also signifies essence, as the Father is God and deity itself.
claims: Augustine speaks of 'person' by its mode of signifying, as substance.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e263.summary: This also answers the second argument, about Boethius's definition.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e266.summary: Likewise for the third argument: although 'person' signifies relation, it does not signify it by way of relation, so it is not referred to another by its name.
claims: 'Person' signifies relation but not by way of relation.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e269.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. 'What' sometimes asks about essence ('what is man? a rational mortal animal') and sometimes about the supposit ('what swims in the sea? a fish'). The answer to the heretics asking 'three what?' was 'persons' in the latter sense.
claims: 'Quid' can ask for the supposit as well as the essence.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e272.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. 'Person' as 'one through itself' signifies not essential unity but the unity of a person, which comes from the property, so the argument is beside the point.
claims: Per se una refers to personal unity from the property.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e275.summary: This also answers the sed contra arguments, which concern what 'person' signifies. In God there are four modes of signifying: the absolute by way of the absolute ('God'), relation by way of relation ('Father'), the absolute by way of relation ('power of begetting'), and the related by way of the absolute ('person'). This happens because relation is essentially the divine substance itself.
claims: Divine names have four modes: absolute as absolute, relative as relative, absolute as relative, relative as absolute ('person').
concepts: four modes of signifying in God

ta-l1d23q1-d1e288.summary: First argument that 'person' is not predicated plurally. According to the text, to be three persons is to be three somethings (tria quaedam), but Father, Son, and Spirit are not granted to be three things, only one.
claims: 'Three persons' would be 'three things'.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e291.summary: Second argument. 'Person' signifies what exists substantially in some nature, and a distinction of properties does not diversify what is substantially in a nature. Father, Son, and Spirit are distinguished only by properties.
claims: Property distinction does not diversify substance.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e294.summary: Third argument. Personal properties are no more substantially in God than essential properties like goodness and wisdom, which do not make several persons.
claims: Essential properties do not multiply persons.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e298.summary: Fourth argument. As 'God' signifies one having the divine nature, 'person' signifies what subsists in the divine nature. Because of the unity of nature there are not several gods, so for the same reason there are not several persons.
claims: 'Deus' and 'persona' both signify one in the divine nature.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e301.summary: Sed contra from Lombard's text and the common usage of the Church.
claims: The Church speaks of three persons.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e304.summary: Second sed contra from Richard of St Victor: those who fear where there is no fear would rightly fear persons being said according to substance if 'person' signified only substantial being and co-signified nothing else, which is why persons are multiplied.
claims: 'Person' co-signifies something beyond substance, which allows plurality.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e310.summary: Thomas's determination. A person is something distinct subsisting in intellectual nature, so wherever there are several distinct beings having intellectual nature, there are several persons, whether or not they share the same nature. That nature is divided among several persons in humans comes from the imperfection of human nature, which is not its own being but receives being in its supposit, so it is in different supposits by different being, and from the mode of distinction, since human persons are distinguished by matter, which is part of the essence, so distinct persons cannot have one essence. Neither holds of the divine persons, so three persons subsist in one nature.
claims: Wherever there are several distinct intellectual subsistents there are several persons, whether or not they share a nature.
Human persons have divided natures because human nature is not its being and they are distinguished by matter; neither holds in God.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e313.summary: Reply to the first argument. Augustine loosely uses 'tria' for 'tres', as Hilary says they are three (tria) by substance and one by harmony, taking substance for hypostasis. Alternatively, they are not three things simply, but 'three somethings', namely three supposits.
claims: The persons are not three things simply but three supposits.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e316.summary: Reply to the second argument. In creatures diversity of properties does not make several persons, since a property is not a subsistent person, but in God the properties are the subsistent persons themselves: paternity is the Father, and to be Father and to be God are not different beings, since there is no being of the Father that is not the Son's. So the number of persons follows the number of personal properties.
claims: In God properties are the subsistent persons, so the persons are numbered by the properties.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e320.summary: Reply to the third argument. Essential properties are also subsistent, but one is not distinguished from another really, only conceptually, whereas relative properties are distinguished by the power of opposition. As the Father is something subsistent, so is the good, but Father and Son are different subsistents, while good and wise are one and the same subsistent, so all these are said of each person. Essential properties do not make a number of persons, since number follows distinction.
claims: Only opposed relative properties distinguish subsistents; essential properties are one subsistent.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e323.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Substantive names are pluralized only by multiplication of the form from which they are imposed. Deity, from which 'God' is imposed, is not multiplied, so neither is 'God'. 'Person' is imposed from the form of personality, which signifies the character of subsisting in such a nature, so where there are several subsistents there are several personalities and several persons.
claims: 'God' is not pluralized because deity is one; 'person' is pluralized because personality is multiplied with subsistents.

ta-l1d23q1-d1e332.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'It is not one thing to be God and another to be person' holds not only by real identity, since in God there is one being, but conceptually too, since a person in God is so called by having subsistent being in the divine nature. What this per se belongs to is relation as subsistent and distinct, since nothing else of this kind can be posited in God. So by mode of signifying 'person' belongs among substantial names, while by what it supposits for in God it belongs among relative ones. (2) 'We say nothing other than the substance of the Father', with substance understood as hypostasis, not essence; Lombard's addition 'the Father is the divine essence' is not explicit in Augustine but is true by real identity, since hypostasis and essence are really the same in God. (3) 'Not to say it, but so as not to be silent' seems to mean 'three persons' is not properly said. Nothing can be said of God properly in our words that perfectly expresses divine truth, but this came into use by necessity, like other things we say of God; since it was not found in canonical Scripture, they would not have dared to use it had necessity not compelled them, so necessity excuses presumption rather than falsity. (4) 'God is thought more truly than he is said' seems false, since we say many things of God that we do not understand (Chrysostom), but though the heart does not reach such things by understanding, it holds them by faith, which it cannot express perfectly (Dist. 39). (5) 'Because Scripture does not contradict it' seems insufficient, since it would not contradict 'one person' either, but Augustine is giving not the whole reason why it is properly said, only why it does not conflict with the piety of faith. (6) He feared to say 'three essences' lest any diversity be understood in that supreme equality; nothing in 'essence' can be drawn toward relation, so a plurality of things would require division in absolutes, not distinction of relations. (7) Hilary proves both unity of essence and plurality of persons: naming the Father separately from the Son shows distinction, excluding a singular God, as if deity were in one supposit only, and a 'unique' God, i.e. solitary, as if there were no companionship of persons by union of love; the unity of essence is proved by the consequence of vision, since whoever sees the Son sees the Father.
claims: 'Person' is substantial by mode of signifying and relative by what it supposits for in God.
'Three persons' was adopted by necessity, which excuses presumption, not falsity.
God is thought more truly than said, held by faith beyond expression.

ta-l1d23q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 23 introduces the exception of 'person' from the rule for essential names, since it is substantial yet plural, and Lombard's explanation from the necessity of answering 'three what?'. It announces four articles on essence, subsistence, substance, and person, the propriety of 'person' in God, its signification, and its plurality.
claims: 'Person' is substantial yet plural.

ta-l1d23q1-Dd1e123.summary: Article 1 distinguishes essence, subsistence, substance, and person (usia, usiosis, hypostasis, prosopon). Rejecting distinctions based on common versus distinct or on quo est and quod est as such, Thomas follows Boethius in distinguishing the first three by the acts they are named from: to be, to subsist, and to stand under. Each can be taken as quo est (form of the whole, form of the part, matter) or as quod est (thing having being, having absolute being, underlying accidents). Essence taken precisively (humanity) is a part and taken non-precisively (man) is the whole. 'Person' is a particular substance of intellectual nature under a property of dignity, named from theatrical masks. The Latin Fathers transposed 'substance' and 'subsistence' relative to the Greek to avoid misunderstanding.
claims: Essence, subsistence, and substance are distinguished by esse, subsistere, and substare, each taken as quo est or quod est.
'Person' is an individual substance of intellectual nature under a property of dignity.

ta-l1d23q1-Dd1e170.summary: Article 2 asks whether 'person' is properly said of God. It is, more nobly than of creatures, as subsisting through itself in intellectual nature. A name is judged by what it is imposed to signify, not by what it is imposed from (theatrical masks). Composition is incidental to personhood, God stands under properties only in our mode of understanding (hence Richard's 'existences'), and 'person' is said of God by completeness, not particularity.
claims: 'Person' is said properly of God by the concept of completeness in intellectual nature.
concepts: id a quo vs. id ad quod

ta-l1d23q1-Dd1e217.summary: Article 3 asks whether 'person' signifies substance or relation. After surveying equivocal and univocal theories, Thomas holds that 'person' in itself signifies an individual intellectual substance and in God signifies what is distinct existing in the divine nature. Since the distinguishing relation is itself the distinct, subsistent person, 'person' in God signifies relation by way of substance, the supposit having the essence. Deity, God, paternity, and Father by their concepts do not have the character of person, though the Father is a person as the Father who is God. The rival theories are each partly true, and divine names have four modes of signifying, 'person' being the relative signified absolutely.
claims: 'Person' in God signifies relation by way of substance, the subsistent relation having the essence.
Divine names signify in four modes; 'person' signifies the relative as absolute.

ta-l1d23q1-Dd1e280.summary: Article 4 asks whether 'person' is predicated plurally. Thomas holds that wherever there are several distinct intellectual subsistents there are several persons, whether or not they share a nature. Humans divide their nature because human nature is not its own being and they are individuated by matter, neither of which holds in God. In God the relative properties are subsistent persons, distinguished by opposition, while essential properties are one subsistent. 'God' is not pluralized because deity is one, but 'person' is, because personality is multiplied with subsistents.
claims: There are three persons in one nature, since persons are numbered by opposed subsistent relations.
'Person' is pluralized by multiplication of personality; 'God' is not.

ta-l1d23q1-Dd1e327.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 23 explains that 'person' is substantial by mode of signifying and relative by what it supposits for in God, and that 'three persons' was adopted by necessity, which excuses presumption rather than falsity. It glosses Augustine's and Hilary's remarks on the inexpressibility of God, the avoidance of 'three essences', and the exclusion of singularity and solitude.
claims: 'Person' is substantial in mode, relative in supposition.

ta-l1d23q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 23 is Thomas's treatment of the name 'person'. Article 1 distinguishes essence, subsistence, and substance, following Boethius, by the acts of being, subsisting, and standing under, each taken as quo est or quod est. It defines person as an individual substance of intellectual nature under a property of dignity and explains the Latin–Greek terminological correspondences. Article 2 holds that 'person' is properly said of God, by the concept of completeness in intellectual nature rather than particularity, since names are judged by what they signify, not their origin. Article 3 holds that 'person' in God signifies relation by way of substance: the distinguishing relation, which is the subsistent person having the divine essence. Article 4 holds that 'person' is predicated plurally because personality is multiplied with distinct subsistents, which in God are the opposed relations, while 'God' remains singular because deity is one.
claims: Essence, subsistence, and substance are distinguished by esse, subsistere, and substare.
'Person' is properly said of God and signifies relation by way of substance.
There are three persons in one nature, numbered by opposed subsistent relations.
